The First Five Days: A Government Remade at Speed

In under a week, a new administration rewrote citizenship rules, emptied out oversight offices, pardoned hundreds convicted of attacking the Capitol, and tested how much of the federal government can be changed by signature alone.

```markdown The second Trump administration did not begin with a transition period. It began with a flood. In the space of five days, the federal government was reordered across immigration, civil rights, energy policy, and the machinery of oversight itself, mostly through unilateral executive action signed before opposition could organize a response. By week's end, courts had already intervened on at least one front, but on most others, policy changes had taken hold in the real world well before any legal challenge could catch up.

**The Weekend**

The pace was set on inauguration day itself. Trump signed dozens of executive orders in a single sitting, touching immigration, energy, diversity programs, federal hiring, and the structure of government — more first-day orders than any modern president had issued. The volume was itself a strategy: by acting simultaneously across nearly every domain of federal policy, the administration made it difficult for Congress, courts, or the public to focus resistance on any single front. Paired with this was the declaration of simultaneous national emergencies at the southern border and over domestic energy production, unlocking military deployment authority, environmental review waivers, and a request for legal advice on invoking the Insurrection Act. Emergency powers meant for genuine crises were being activated as tools for standing policy goals.

Nowhere was the day's ambition clearer than in the treatment of the January 6 Capitol attack. Roughly 1,500 people charged or convicted in connection with the assault — including leaders convicted of seditious conspiracy — received pardons or commutations, and the Justice Department was directed to drop any remaining cases. This was not an isolated act of clemency but the start of a coordinated effort to unwind legal accountability for an attack on Congress, one that would continue later in the week when House Republicans formed a new panel to challenge the findings of the earlier bipartisan investigation into Trump's own culpability.

Also signed that day was an executive order attempting to end birthright citizenship for children born in the United States to undocumented or temporary-visa parents — a direct challenge to the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause. States and civil rights groups sued almost immediately, opening a legal battle that would develop over the following days. Alongside it came Executive Order 14168, declaring that the federal government would recognize only two biological sexes. Its effects cascaded quickly: passport denials, military discharges, exclusion from shelters, and the reassignment of transgender detainees and prisoners according to sex assigned at birth, stripping transgender Americans of federal recognition across multiple systems at once.

Immigration policy shifted just as fast. The CBP One appointment app, used to schedule lawful asylum appointments, was shut down within hours of the inauguration, cancelling roughly 30,000 scheduled appointments without notice or alternative. The border emergency declaration paired this closure with the deployment of active-duty troops and Marines, even though border crossings were then at multi-year lows. Meanwhile, the administration moved against the federal workforce itself, reinstating Schedule F to strip job protections from tens of thousands of policy-influencing employees, freezing federal hiring, and ending remote work — the opening move in a broader effort to make the civil service answerable to political loyalty rather than institutional continuity.

Not every first-day action carried equal weight. Trump directed the Justice Department not to enforce a law — upheld by the Supreme Court — banning TikTok, citing the app's popularity with young voters, a notable instance of an administration declining to enforce a validly enacted statute. The United States also began withdrawing from the Paris climate accord and the World Health Organization, while a national energy emergency expedited fossil fuel permitting and rolled back electric-vehicle and offshore-wind policy. DEI programs across the federal government were eliminated, staff placed on leave, and a 1965 nondiscrimination requirement for federal contractors was revoked. Smaller but telling moves rounded out the weekend: security clearances were stripped from roughly 50 former intelligence officials and John Bolton over a 2020 letter regarding Hunter Biden's laptop, and Trump and Melania Trump launched personal cryptocurrency tokens just before and after the inauguration, reportedly generating billions in paper value with promotion from exchanges under federal investigation.

**Tuesday**

By Tuesday, the government had moved from declaration to implementation. The Department of Homeland Security rescinded guidance that had limited immigration enforcement near sensitive locations, opening schools, churches, and hospitals to arrest, and raids intensified in communities near Mar-a-Lago and elsewhere. At the State Department, deputy assistant secretaries in the Bureau of Consular Affairs were removed the morning after inauguration and replaced with members of an ideologically aligned, immigration-restrictionist fellowship — an early sign that career expertise across the foreign service would be subordinated to political loyalty. DEI policy moved from proclamation to agency-level execution, with Executive Order 14173 directing formal termination of diversity practices and the revocation of the 1965 Equal Employment Opportunity order that had underpinned federal contractor nondiscrimination requirements for sixty years. The National Treasury Employees Union filed suit against Schedule F that same day, and Democratic state attorneys general began a wave of litigation against the administration's executive orders, while a public-interest law firm sued over the newly created Department of Government Efficiency for alleged transparency violations. Litigation, rather than legislative pushback, was emerging as the primary check on the pace of executive action.

**Wednesday**

Attention turned to the press and to internal purges. The new FCC chairman reinstated Trump campaign complaints against ABC, NBC, and CBS over alleged election coverage bias and reopened an investigation into CBS's editing of a Kamala Harris interview — a probe later leveraged during review of a corporate merger. Enrique Tarrio, the Proud Boys leader convicted of seditious conspiracy, was pardoned and released, emboldening far-right groups even as the Justice Department's national security and criminal divisions saw senior career officials removed and reassigned. A presidential memorandum restructured National Security Council decision-making, and dozens of acting officials were installed across agencies, sidestepping normal Senate confirmation timelines. Smaller actions that day included a Foreign Terrorist Organization designation for the Houthis and a $2 billion investment in Jared Kushner's private equity firm from Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund, made over the objection of the fund's own investment committee.

**Thursday**

Thursday brought the week's clearest judicial rebuke. U.S. District Judge John Coughenour issued a temporary restraining order blocking the birthright citizenship executive order, calling it "blatantly unconstitutional" — a rare instance of a court moving as quickly as the administration itself, and evidence that some constitutional limits remained enforceable even amid the surrounding velocity of change. The same day, House Republicans formally launched their new select subcommittee to revisit January 6, aiming to challenge the conclusions of the earlier bipartisan investigation. An executive order deregulating cryptocurrency followed days after the president's own crypto ventures launched, revoking consumer protections and establishing a Presidential Working Group on Digital Asset Markets. Smaller developments rounded out the day: the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology was reestablished under new leadership, assassination records related to JFK, RFK, and Martin Luther King Jr. were ordered declassified, a House resolution proposed amending the two-term presidential limit in terms that would exclude a prior president while opening a path for a third Trump term, and Purdue Pharma reached a $7.4 billion opioid settlement with the Sackler family — one of the week's few developments unconnected to the administration's own agenda.

**Friday**

The week closed with two of its most consequential moves. The administration fired at least 12 inspectors general across major federal agencies in a single action, reportedly without the 30-day congressional notice required by law — removing internal watchdogs en masse before their oversight of the week's other actions could even begin. Separately, Trump threatened to withhold wildfire disaster relief from California unless the state adopted mandatory voter ID requirements and altered its water policy, tying humanitarian aid to unrelated political demands against a state governed by the opposing party. An executive order reasserted Hyde Amendment restrictions on federal abortion funding, extending the week's broader pattern of reproductive-rights reversal. The Senate confirmed Pete Hegseth as defense secretary by a 50-50 vote broken by Vice President JD Vance, despite allegations of sexual assault and financial mismanagement and opposition from two Republican senators — a confirmation that tested how far the Senate's advice-and-consent function could bend under party pressure. A FEMA Review Council was established the same day, following Trump's public suggestion that disaster response might shift entirely to the states.

**The Week in Sum**

Across the five days, several threads ran continuously beneath the surface of individual headlines. Executive action consistently outpaced the capacity of Congress, courts, and the public to respond in real time. Accountability for the January 6 attack was both legally erased through pardons and historically contested through a new congressional panel. Immigration enforcement moved from a system of prioritized targeting toward something closer to a dragnet, with legal pathways closed and enforcement zones widened into schools and hospitals. Transgender Americans lost federal recognition across passports, the military, shelters, and prisons within days. And the internal watchdogs meant to check all of this — inspectors general, career civil servants, career diplomats — were removed or restructured before they could act. Against all of it, the first institutional counterweights appeared just as quickly: a federal judge blocking an unconstitutional order, a union suing over civil-service protections, state attorneys general filing challenge after challenge. The week did not resolve any of these contests. It set their terms — a pattern of speed, volume, and unilateral action, met by a pattern of litigation as the first line of response — that would recur throughout the term to come. ```
